content: Keloids are an abnormal overgrowth of scar tissue that develops at the site of a healed skin injury. They are characterized by their raised, thickened appearance and can extend beyond the boundaries of the original wound. Symptoms of Keloids: Keloids typically present as skin lesions that may be flesh-colored, red, or pink. They are often located directly over the site of a previous wound or injury. The lesions may appear lumpy (nodular) or ridged in texture. During their formation and growth, keloids may cause itching. Causes of Keloids: Keloids can develop as a result of various skin injuries, including: Acne Burns Chickenpox Ear piercings Minor scratches Surgical incisions Traumatic wounds Vaccination sites Risk Factors: Keloids are more commonly observed in individuals aged 10 to 20 years. They are also more prevalent among African Americans, Asians, and Hispanics. A family history of keloids increases the likelihood of their occurrence. The term keloidosis is used when multiple or recurrent keloids are present. Diagnosis: The diagnosis of keloids is primarily based on the clinical appearance of the skin or scar. In some cases, a skin biopsy may be performed to exclude other types of skin growths, such as tumors. When to Seek Medical Attention: You should contact your healthcare provider if: You develop keloids and wish to explore options for their removal or reduction. You experience new symptoms associated with keloids. Treatment Options: Keloids often do not require treatment unless they cause discomfort or cosmetic concerns. However, their size may be reduced through the following methods: Corticosteroid injections Cryotherapy (freezing) Laser treatments Radiation therapy Surgical removal Prognosis: Keloids are generally not medically dangerous, but they can affect a person’s appearance. Over time, some keloids may become smaller, flatter, and less noticeable, though this process can take several years. Exposure to sunlight during the first year after a keloid forms can cause it to darken permanently compared to the surrounding skin. Surgical removal of a keloid does not guarantee permanent resolution, as it may lead to the formation of a larger keloid scar. Potential Complications: Keloids can lead to several complications, including: Cosmetic changes that impact appearance Discomfort or tenderness in the keloid area Irritation caused by friction with clothing or other surfaces Limited mobility if the keloids are extensive Psychological distress, particularly if the keloid is large or disfiguring Recurrence of the keloid after treatment Prevention: To prevent discoloration from sun exposure, cover the forming keloid with a patch or Band-Aid and use sunscreen when spending time outdoors. These protective measures should be continued for at least six months after an injury or surgery in adults, and up to 18 months in children.
